Research

Two questions I did not like the easy answer to

Both started as an assumption everyone shared. Both turned out to be wrong, and in each case the wrongness was the finding.

01 · Fairness in melanoma detection

Paper title

Adding Darker Skin Tone Images Does Not Improve Fairness in Melanoma Detection: A Controlled Study Extending the Pipsqueak Analysis

Co-authored with Noor Ul Huda Batool · Department of Computer Science, COMSATS University Islamabad · August 2026 · three-phase controlled comparison · MobileNetV2 on Kaggle dermoscopy and the Diverse Dermatology Images set, with skin tone measured by Individual Typology Angle and validated against Fitzpatrick labels.

Skin cancer apps work noticeably worse on darker skin. Almost everyone agrees why: the training photos are overwhelmingly of light skin, so the obvious fix is to add more images of darker skin. I ran a controlled study to test whether that fix actually works.

It did not. Adding real darker-skin photographs to the training data made the model worse on darker skin, not better, dropping its accuracy on healthy dark skin from 81% to 64%. I ran the same experiment with lighter-skin photos as a control, and that degraded too. So the problem was never really about who was in the photos.

The real problem is that the two sets of photos are different kinds of picture. The model learned from tight clinical close-ups of a single mole, but real people upload wider phone photos with skin and background around it. It is like training someone on passport photos and then asking them to identify faces in holiday snaps. Until that gap is closed, adding more diverse data cannot help, because the model cannot read either kind reliably.

This matters because it changes what you should spend effort on. Collecting more diverse images is slow, expensive and ethically delicate, and this study suggests it will not fix the problem on its own. The paper is written up in full with the method, the numbers and an honest list of what it does not prove.

02 · Which pages should a content team fix first?

Paper title

Refresh and Content Opportunity Scoring: Ranking Pages for Human Review Under Limited Capacity

FlyRank machine learning internship capstone, 2026 · 30,000 content pages, 44 columns, 32 pseudonymised clients · data contract verified against a 9,841,378-row warehouse release.

A content team can only review so many pages a week. I asked whether ordinary search, content and freshness signals can tell them which pages to open first. I set it up as a straight yes-or-no question about whether a page had declined, built a plain staleness-and-visibility baseline to beat, then trained a logistic regression and scored both on the same held-out pages, split so that no client in the test set ever appeared in training.

The model looked excellent. Then, while writing the paper, I ran a third check for leakage and found something my first two checks had missed: the answer was sitting inside my own inputs. The decline label is defined from two impression columns, and both were still features. I had excluded a trend column by name and assumed that was enough. It had excluded nothing.

Removing those columns took Average Precision from 0.87 to 0.60 and Precision@50 from a perfect 1.00 down to 0.70. That is the real number, and it is still clearly better than the baseline on every measure. I published both sets side by side, because the gap between them is the actual result: it is what a leak looks like when you catch it.

What this gives a content team is a sensible order to work through, nothing more. It does not explain why a page declined, and it is not a guess at how Google ranks anything.
